title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers

paper.title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models have emerged as the foundation of modern generative systems, yet their high memorization capacity raises privacy concerns. While differentially private (DP) training provides formal guarantees, it comes at a cost in sample quality.
In this work, we study a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred during the sampling process itself? Directly analyzing modern neural denoisers is challenging because their sensitivity to a single training example is generally intractable. To overcome this challenge, we construct and analyze a clipped privacy-accountable empirical denoiser , a training-free estimator of the Bayes-optimal denoiser, whose per-step sensitivity can be computed explicitly, allowing each denoising step to be a Gaussian mechanism. This perspective enables privacy accounting under Gaussian DP when each training example contributes to each denoising step, and under f f -DP trade-off functions when each generated sample uses a single randomly subsampled block of the training data. We report every ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) guarantee as a certified upper bound from a privacy loss distribution accountant, and use a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation as a fast diagnostic, characterizing where it is reliable and where it becomes anti-conservative. We also analyze the privacy loss along the denoising trajectory and show that it grows steeply near the critical window in which semantic content is formed. This observation motivates hybrid samplers that use the private empirical denoiser through the formative steps where it remains a faithful proxy for the neural denoiser, then switch to a public neural denoiser for the remaining refinement. Our results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 show that the privacy of diffusion models depends not only on the training procedure, but also on sampling-time design choices such as subsampling, stopping time, and hybrid denoising.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) are now central to modern generative systems, but their ability to reproduce training examples raises serious privacy concerns ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Carlini et al., 2023 ; Tang et al., 2024 ; Hu & Pang, 2023 ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Matsumoto et al., 2023 ) . Post-hoc filters and memorization-aware model changes can reduce visible leakage, but they do not give attack-agnostic privacy guarantees. Differentially private (DP) training gives such guarantees, but it answers a different question: it bounds what the weights reveal, while users and regulators see only generated samples. Sampling-time leakage is a separate surface that persists even when the denoiser is trained non-privately, whether or not DP training is practical at scale. This raises a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred by the sampling process itself? Answering this requires treating the sampler, rather than the training algorithm, as the mechanism to be analyzed. The obstacle is that a neural denoiser has intractable data sensitivity, so its denoising steps admit no explicit privacy accounting. To make the problem analyzable, we privatize an empirical denoiser ( Niedoba et al., 2025 ) whose sensitivity can be computed directly. Since each reverse diffusion step already injects Gaussian noise, the empirical denoising update can be interpreted as a Gaussian mechanism, allowing us to track the sampling trajectory with Gaussian Differential Privacy (GDP) ( Dong et al., 2022 ) . However, the GDP composition using the full batch of training data yields a poor privacy level. Denoising with subsampled data at each denoising step can improve the privacy level. However, this hurts the diffusion sampling, as every newly drawn subset of data injects extra stochastic drift into the sampling trajectory, which prevents coherent semantics from forming across the trajectory. To this end, we propose output-wise subsampling , subsample a block from the dataset once and reuse it for the entire denoising trajectory to produce one sample. This stabilizes the denoising direction and achieves a decent privacy level. When converting f f -DP to ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -DP, we encounter unreliable conversion, especially at small δ \delta , when using the CLT-type f f -DP accounting that assumes the CDF of the standardized test statistic under the composition is simply Gaussian. We report all guarantees as certified upper bounds from a PLD accountant ( Doroshenko et al., 2022 ) , and study a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation ( Zheng et al., 2020 ) as a fast estimate and measure where it is accurate and where it understates the certified value. Our contributions are summarized below: 1. We privatize a clipped empirical denoiser with explicit per-step sensitivity of 2 ​ C / | 𝒟 | 2C/|\mathcal{D}| . Diffusion sampling then becomes a composition of Gaussian mechanisms, with no model trained on the private data. 2. We derive privacy guarantees for full-batch and output-wise subsampled diffusion sampling using GDP and f f -DP trade-off functions, and report certified ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) upper bounds from a PLD accountant. We use the Edgeworth approximation as a diagnostic where cumulant checks pass, and characterize where it fails. Subsampling amplification applies once per reused block, rather than once per step. 3. We show that the per-step privacy cost grows along the trajectory relative to the critical window, measure where the empirical denoiser is a window-local semantic proxy for a neural denoiser, and use both to place the private-to-public handoff, evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64.

sections.heading: 2.2 Differential Privacy and Gaussian Mechanism
sections.text: Differential Privacy (DP) provides a formal framework to limit the influence of any single record on the output of a randomized algorithm. Intuitively, whether or not an individual’s data is present, the distribution of outputs should remain (almost) unchanged. This view naturally extends to diffusion sampling, which is itself a randomized mechanism. A fundamental building block is the Gaussian mechanism : given a function h : 𝒟 ↦ ℝ p h:\mathcal{D}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{p} , the mechanism releases ℳ Gauss ​ ( 𝒟 , h ) = h ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) + 𝒏 , 𝒏 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ​ Δ h 2 ​ 𝐈 ) , \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Gauss}}(\mathcal{D};h)=h(\mathcal{D})+\bm{n},\qquad\bm{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\Delta_{h}^{2}\mathbf{I}), (2) where Δ h \Delta_{h} is the global sensitivity—the maximum change in h h between neighboring datasets. By calibrating the noise to Δ h \Delta_{h} , the Gaussian mechanism guarantees DP (see Appendix H.1 for formal definitions). For analyzing multi-step procedures such as diffusion sampling, we adopt Gaussian Differential Privacy (GDP) ( Dong et al., 2022 ) . GDP tightly characterizes the privacy loss of Gaussian mechanisms and, crucially, admits an exact composition rule: μ = ∑ i μ i 2 , \displaystyle\mu=\sqrt{\sum_{i}\mu_{i}^{2}}, (3) where μ i \mu_{i} is the GDP parameter of the i i -th step. For example, in the case of eq. 2 with 𝒏 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ​ Δ 𝒉 2 ​ 𝐈 ) \bm{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\Delta_{{\bm{h}}}^{2}\mathbf{I}) , the Gaussian mechanism corresponds to μ i \mu_{i} -GDP with μ i = 1 σ \mu_{i}=\frac{1}{\sigma} . This makes GDP especially well-suited for diffusion processes, which inject Gaussian noise at every denoising step. Two further facts are important for our analysis. First, privacy amplification by subsampling can further reduce the effective μ \mu . Second, GDP parameters can be translated into ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) guarantees when needed for regulatory reporting; we provide details in Appendix H.2 . Together, these tools allow us to connect the denoising process directly to established DP accounting methods.

sections.heading: 3.3 Bridging Empirical and Neural Denoisers
sections.text: A central limitation is that real diffusion samplers use neural denoisers, while our formal accounting uses an empirical denoiser. Directly accounting for neural denoisers remains open because the sensitivity of a trained network to one training example is not tractable. We therefore use the empirical denoiser as an analyzable proxy and check where this proxy is informative. First, Figure 1 shows that empirical and neural denoising directions are nearly aligned on CIFAR-10 in the earlier stages of the denoising process. Second, recent work on critical windows ( Li & Chen, 2024 ; Biroli et al., 2024 ; Sclocchi et al., 2024 ; Georgiev et al., 2023 ; Raya & Ambrogioni, 2023 ) suggests that coarse semantic identity is determined early and then remains stable, so the formative part of the trajectory overlaps with the regime where the two denoisers are most similar. Together, these checks do not prove a neural-denoiser DP guarantee, but they justify using the empirical accountant to study where sampling leakage occurs. Cosine similarity captures only the denoising direction ; the per-step magnitude gap ‖ 𝔼 ^ − D ‖ 2 \|\widehat{\mathbb{E}}-D\|^{2} is reported in Appendix F , where it peaks inside the mid-noise window, but as Table 1 shows, does not survive to the released sample. We therefore restrict the proxy claim to directional agreement over the regime our private block occupies.

sections.heading: 4 Privacy Analysis of Denoising Process with Subsampled Data
sections.text: Section 3 analyzes the empirical denoiser when every record in 𝒟 \mathcal{D} contributes to every private denoising step. This full-batch accountant is tight, but it is expensive in terms of privacy: each generated output repeatedly touches every record, and privacy loss grows quickly when many outputs are released. Subsampling reduces this exposure because a record that is not selected contributes no privacy loss. Throughout, each generated output draws a minibatch 𝒮 ⊆ 𝒟 \mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{D} of fixed size B B uniformly without replacement, so a fixed record is included with probability q ℬ = B / n q_{\mathcal{B}}=B/n , and neighboring datasets differ by adding or removing one record. Because | 𝒮 | = B |\mathcal{S}|=B is fixed, an added record that is selected takes the place of another record of 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , so within the minibatch the change is a replacement ( Zhu et al., 2022 ; Lebeda et al., 2025 ) . The clipped minibatch average therefore has sensitivity 2 ​ C / B 2C/B , and each step is μ t \mu_{t} -GDP with μ t = 2 ​ C β ​ B ​ 2 ​ Δ ​ t / t 3 \mu_{t}=\frac{2C}{\beta B}\sqrt{2\Delta t/t^{3}} conditional on inclusion. The subsampled Gaussian mechanism is ℳ SubGauss ​ ( 𝒟 , 𝒙 t ) = | 𝒮 | − 1 ​ ∑ 𝒙 0 ∈ 𝒮 𝐯 ¯ ​ ( 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 t ) + β ​ t 3 / ( 2 ​ Δ ​ t ) ​ ϵ \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SubGauss}}(\mathcal{D};{\bm{x}}_{t})=|\mathcal{S}|^{-1}\sum_{{\bm{x}}_{0}\in\mathcal{S}}\bar{\mathbf{v}}({\bm{x}}_{0};{\bm{x}}_{t})+\beta\sqrt{t^{3}/(2\Delta t)}\,\bm{\epsilon} . The important design choice is how often we resample 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . Resampling at every denoising step for every output gives more independent amplification events, but it also changes the empirical denoising direction at every step. Small minibatches, which is better for privacy, inject extra stochastic drift into the reverse trajectory: the sample is repeatedly pulled toward different private subsets, and late low-noise steps are especially sensitive to this instability, as shown in Figure 2 . This can harm sample quality even though the privacy accountant looks attractive. We therefore employ output-wise subsampling : sample once for a generated output, reuse them through an empirical denoising block, then account for amplification once at the block level. This keeps the denoising direction stable while still limiting how often any record is accessed. We state both accountants because they correspond to different mechanisms. Applying per-step amplification to output-wise subsampling would be incorrect: privacy amplification is tied to independent subsampling events, not to the number of denoising steps. If the same minibatch is reused over a block ℬ \mathcal{B} , the included record accumulates the full block-level Gaussian parameter μ ¯ ℬ = ( ∑ t ∈ ℬ μ t 2 ) 1 / 2 \bar{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}}=(\sum_{t\in\mathcal{B}}\mu_{t}^{2})^{1/2} before amplification is applied. If a fresh minibatch is drawn at every step, each μ t \mu_{t} is amplified separately. For full-batch Gaussian mechanisms, GDP composition is exact. With subsampling, each block’s trade-off curve is a mixture rather than a Gaussian curve, so exact GDP composition no longer applies, and we compose numerically with a pessimistic PLD accountant (Section 2.3 ). The GDP central limit theorem ( Dong et al., 2022 ) fits poorly here because the μ t \mu_{t} are highly heterogeneous, and its Berry-Esseen error is additive and too coarse for small δ \delta (Table 11 ). As a fast estimate, we also compute a degree-two Edgeworth approximation ( Zheng et al., 2020 ) , which adds skewness and kurtosis corrections from the first four cumulants (eq. 25 , Appendix D ). It is an approximation and matches the certified PLD value to within 1% for ε ≤ 2 \varepsilon\leq 2 but understates it for larger ε \varepsilon , by up to 15% in our runs (Appendix G ). sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Differentially private training has been the most direct approach to reduce memorization in diffusion models. DP training of diffusion models builds on DP-SGD ( Abadi et al., 2016 ; Dockhorn et al., 2023 ; Ghalebikesabi et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) and protects the weights at a cost in sample quality. Private sampling has mostly been studied for Bayesian posterior inference, where the samples are model parameters rather than data ( Welling & Teh, 2011 ; Wang et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2019 ; Räisä et al., 2021 ; Zhang & Zhang, 2023 ) . Bertazzi et al. (2025) show that privacy loss in SGLD can concentrate in the final step, but their analysis needs strongly convex, Lipschitz objectives, which our empirical denoiser does not satisfy.

sections.heading: Sampling-time privacy for diffusion models.
sections.text: Closest to our setting, Sehwag et al. (2023) also analyze privacy at generation rather than training time, clip denoiser outputs, treat each step as a Gaussian mechanism, and delegate late denoising to a public model. Our analysis differs in three respects. First, their per-step sensitivity C / k C/k arises from a sample-and-aggregate ensemble of k k non-private models trained on disjoint shards, so the sensitivity floor is set by the ensemble size and private training is still required; we obtain sensitivity 2 ​ C / | 𝒟 | 2C/|\mathcal{D}| by clipping individual contributions to a single empirical average, with no training at all. Second, they adopt a per-sample private-prediction threat model and name composition across multiple released samples as open; we give an explicit joint-release guarantee over N out N_{\mathrm{out}} outputs under standard DP, using subsampled f f -DP with block-level amplification. Third, we localize privacy loss to the critical window and place the handoff at the measured crossover rather than at a fixed schedule fraction, validating the choice with a membership-inference proxy. Wei et al. (2023) study inherent privacy properties of discrete denoising diffusion and likewise find that leakage concentrates at particular stages of generation. Their mechanism is the discrete transition kernel, while ours is the continuous Gaussian reverse SDE, where the noise already injected by the sampler serves as the mechanism noise. Our results are therefore a continuous-state counterpart to their staged view, and our claims are scoped accordingly.

sections.heading: Empirical denoisers.
sections.text: Niedoba et al. (2025) characterize the empirical denoiser in the non-private setting and analyze how trained neural denoisers depart from it. We build on this object directly: our contribution is the clipped, privatized variant and its sensitivity analysis, and their non-private characterization is complementary evidence for the proxy argument in Section 3.3 .

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We study (i) full-batch versus subsampled accounting, (ii) where privacy loss accumulates relative to the critical window, and (iii) the privacy-utility trade-off of the hybrid sampler.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: We implement our modified reverse denoising process in PyTorch ( Paszke et al., 2019 ) and categorize our experiments into two regimes: (i) full-batch , where the entire dataset is used in each denoising step, and (ii) output-wise subsampled SDEdit ( Meng et al., 2021 ) , where a minibatch of private examples is subsampled once per generated output and reused for an empirical denoising block. We apply the private empirical denoising steps until time t 0 t_{0} , then add Gaussian noise with scale ( σ t 1 2 − σ t 0 2 ) 1 / 2 (\sigma_{t_{1}}^{2}-\sigma_{t_{0}}^{2})^{1/2} to move the sample back to an SDEdit restart level t 1 > t 0 t_{1}>t_{0} , and finally complete generation with a public neural denoiser from t 1 t_{1} to 0 0 . Only the empirical subsampled block is privacy-accounted. Re-noising to a higher noise level lets the public neural denoiser correct artifacts introduced by the empirical step while incurring no additional privacy loss by post-processing. We use the EDM schedule ( Karras et al., 2022 ) with σ min = 0.002 \sigma_{\min}=0.002 , σ max = 80 \sigma_{\max}=80 , ρ = 7 \rho=7 , N = 50 N=50 steps for full-batch runs and N = 39 N=39 for the hybrid pipeline, and the public normalization β = 1 \beta=1 (Appendices E and J ).

sections.text: On CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2009 ) ( n = 50,000 n=50{,}000 ) the public denoiser is trained on ImageNet 32 × 32 32\times 32 ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) , and on CelebA 64 × 64 64\times 64 ( Liu et al., 2015 ) ( n = 162,770 n=162{,}770 ) it is trained on FFHQ ( Karras et al., 2019 ) . sections.heading: 6.1 Privacy analysis of diffusion-based sampling with full training data
sections.text: When every record is used at every step, a single sample already costs ε ≈ 200 \varepsilon\approx 200 when denoising down to σ min = 0.1 \sigma_{\min}=0.1 , which is needed for a recognizable sample, and at ε ≈ 1 \varepsilon\approx 1 ( σ min = 5 \sigma_{\min}=5 ) the sample is indistinguishable from noise (Figure 4 , Appendix I ). Since each denoising step operates on the full dataset, the per-sample privacy loss is already high, and composing multiple samples results in a rapidly growing total privacy budget under GDP. Subsampling can alleviate this issue through privacy amplification, making it more suitable for large-scale sample generation.

sections.heading: 6.3 Privacy in relation to the critical windows
sections.text: We extend our privacy analyses to quantify privacy levels based on where we stop relative to the critical window of the denoising process. Following Georgiev et al. (2023) , we locate the critical window with a zero-shot CLIP classifier ( Radford et al., 2021 ) applied along the trajectory (Figure 6 (a)). The probability that the sample is classified as a ship is about 0.1 at t = 0.27 t=0.27 , 0.3 at t = 0.07 t=0.07 , and close to 1 at t = 0.02 t=0.02 (70%, 80%, and 88% of the N = 50 N=50 steps). Stopping the private block earlier gives a smaller μ \mu but a noisier sample, and stopping later gives the reverse (Figure 7 ). We choose the handoff point so that, over the private block, the empirical denoiser remains a faithful stand-in for the neural denoiser. The empirical denoiser is a window-local semantic proxy for the neural denoiser through the mid-noise window, which ends at t = 1.98 t=1.98 , about half of the N = 39 N=39 steps (Table 1 ), and directional agreement stays at cos ≥ 0.98 \cos\geq 0.98 through about 55% of generation (Figure 1 , Table 4 ). A 55% handoff therefore keeps the private block essentially inside the proxy regime. Our 65% handoff ( t 0 ≈ 0.52 t_{0}\approx 0.52 ) still comes before the CLIP-visible critical window ( ≈ 70 {\approx}\,70 – 88 % 88\% ), but its private block covers most of the low-noise window, where substitution moves the endpoint more than re-drawing that window’s noise ( 1.64 × 1.64\times CLIP, Table 1 ). The proxy interpretation is therefore weaker for the 65% block, while the certified privacy guarantee holds for both, because it is a statement about the sampler we run. Stopping earlier tightens the certified bound at a utility cost, and stopping later extends the private block into the low-noise steps that dominate the privacy cost (Appendix J ).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.text: We give certified sampling-time privacy guarantees for continuous diffusion models by privatizing a clipped empirical denoiser. Framing each denoising step as a Gaussian mechanism, we account with GDP and f f -DP, report certified ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) bounds from a PLD accountant, and characterize where Edgeworth approximation is and is not reliable. Our results show that leakage is highly non-uniform across timesteps, concentrating in critical windows where semantic structure emerges, while subsampling significantly amplifies privacy guarantees. These findings suggest that privacy in diffusion models is not solely determined by training but can be shaped by sampling strategies such as early stopping and hybrid use of public denoisers. Our certificate covers the sampler we run. Samplers that query a neural denoiser trained on the private data at every step, and discrete diffusion, where the transition kernel would be the mechanism, remain open. Our sampler could also serve as a DP data-augmentation mechanism 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}) : a model trained only on 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}) and public data is ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) -DP by post-processing, with no DP training algorithm. Since privacy loss concentrates at low noise, training on 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D}) for t ≥ t 0 t\geq t_{0} and on public data for t < t 0 t<t_{0} would spend the budget only on the formative regime.

sections.text: The standard Edgeworth approximation for subsampled Gaussian mechanisms is often stated for the setting where a fresh subsample is drawn at every private step. sections.heading: No lower bound on the sampling rate alone.
sections.text: A small sampling probability q ℬ q_{\mathcal{B}} does not by itself invalidate the Edgeworth approximation. For fixed finite μ ¯ ℬ \bar{\mu}_{\mathcal{B}} , the variance and higher cumulants shrink with powers of q ℬ q_{\mathcal{B}} , and these powers largely cancel after standardization. The relevant question is not whether q ℬ q_{\mathcal{B}} is large, but whether the composed privacy-loss sum has enough effective variance and is not dominated by a small number of blocks.

sections.heading: Variance and dominance checks.
sections.text: First, V P V_{P} and V Q V_{Q} should be positive and numerically stable. If either variance is extremely small, the mechanism may be close to perfect privacy, but the standardized Edgeworth CDF and inverse-CDF calculations become ill-conditioned. Second, no block should dominate the variance: max ℬ ⁡ κ 2 , ℬ P V P ≪ 1 , max ℬ ⁡ κ 2 , ℬ Q V Q ≪ 1 . \displaystyle\max_{\mathcal{B}}\frac{\kappa^{P}_{2,\mathcal{B}}}{V_{P}}\ll 1,\qquad\max_{\mathcal{B}}\frac{\kappa^{Q}_{2,\mathcal{B}}}{V_{Q}}\ll 1. (31) This condition is particularly important for diffusion schedules, where late low-noise timesteps can dominate ∑ t μ t 2 \sum_{t}\mu_{t}^{2} if they are grouped into a large private block.

sections.heading: Standardized cumulants.
sections.text: The Edgeworth correction should be small at the quantiles used for the reported ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) guarantee. We monitor the standardized third and fourth cumulants ρ 3 , P = | K 3 , P | V P 3 / 2 , ρ 4 , P = | K 4 , P | V P 2 , ρ 3 , Q = | K 3 , Q | V Q 3 / 2 , ρ 4 , Q = | K 4 , Q | V Q 2 . \displaystyle\rho_{3,P}=\frac{|K_{3,P}|}{V_{P}^{3/2}},\qquad\rho_{4,P}=\frac{|K_{4,P}|}{V_{P}^{2}},\qquad\rho_{3,Q}=\frac{|K_{3,Q}|}{V_{Q}^{3/2}},\qquad\rho_{4,Q}=\frac{|K_{4,Q}|}{V_{Q}^{2}}. sections.heading: Tail and CDF checks.
sections.text: Very small δ \delta values may require evaluating the approximation close to the boundary of the CDF, where finite-sample Edgeworth approximations are less stable. We therefore check that the approximated CDFs are monotone, remain in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] before substantial clipping or projection, and produce a nonnegative δ ⁡ ( ε ) \delta(\varepsilon) curve in the reported range. sections.heading: H.1 Differential Privacy
sections.text: The concept of differential privacy (DP) ( Abadi et al., 2016 ; Dwork et al., 2006 ) provides a formal guarantee that a model behaves almost identically regardless of whether any particular data sample is included in the training set. In other words, DP bounds the extent to which a single sample can influence the model’s behavior. More precisely, a mechanism ℳ \mathcal{M} , which may be a training algorithm such as Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) or, more generally, any randomized algorithm including diffusion sampling, is said to be ϵ \epsilon -DP if the privacy loss is bounded by ϵ \epsilon : log ⁡ P r [ ℳ ( 𝒟 ) = o ] P r [ ℳ ( 𝒟 ′ ) = o ] ≤ ϵ \log{\frac{Pr[\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D})=o]}{Pr[\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})=o]}}\leq\epsilon , where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and 𝒟 ′ \mathcal{D}^{\prime} differ in the record of a single individual; and ℳ ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) = o \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D})=o denotes that applying the mechanism ℳ \mathcal{M} on a dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} ends up converging to the output event o o . For instance, if ℳ \mathcal{M} is a training optimizer such as SGD, then ℳ ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D}) is the trained model and P ​ r ​ ( ℳ ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) = o ) Pr(\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D})=o) depicts the probability the model o o being the trained one. Intuitively, if deleting a single data point in 𝒟 \mathcal{D} to obtain 𝒟 ′ \mathcal{D}^{\prime} does not substantially change the probability of obtaining the same output model o o , then the training algorithm can be regarded as privacy-preserving 1 1 1 SGD and Adam are not DP algorithms as the gradient update may be dominated by a huge outlier that significantly affects the model’s parameters. As a result, a model trained with SGD/Adam can potentially reveal information about such outliers, leaving the data vulnerable to extraction attacks. . Put more simply, if the probability the model converges to the same parameters is relatively equivalent regardless of whether a particular sample is present, then that sample cannot be said to meaningfully affect training. More generally, ℳ \mathcal{M} is ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) -DP if for all neighboring 𝒟 , 𝒟 ′ \mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime} and every measurable set of outputs O O , Pr [ ℳ ( 𝒟 ) ∈ O ] ≤ e ε Pr [ ℳ ( 𝒟 ′ ) ∈ O ] + δ . \displaystyle\text{Pr}[\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D})\in O]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\text{Pr}[\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\in O]+\delta. (40) The privacy-loss condition Pr [ log Pr [ ℳ ( 𝒟 ) = o ] Pr [ ℳ ( 𝒟 ′ ) = o ] ≥ ε ] ≤ δ \text{Pr}\big[\log\frac{\text{Pr}[\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D})=o]}{\text{Pr}[\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime})=o]}\geq\varepsilon\big]\leq\delta implies eq. 40 but is not equivalent to it. A natural building block for designing private (either training or sampling) algorithms is the Gaussian mechanism . This is particularly relevant for our setting, since each step in diffusion sampling injects Gaussian noise. Formally, given a function 𝒉 : 𝒟 ↦ ℝ p {\bm{h}}:\mathcal{D}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{p} , the Gaussian mechanism releases ℳ Gauss ​ ( 𝒟 , 𝒉 ) = 𝒉 ⁡ ( 𝒟 ) + 𝒏 , \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Gauss}}(\mathcal{D};{\bm{h}})={\bm{h}}(\mathcal{D})+\bm{n}, (41) where 𝒏 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ​ Δ 𝒉 2 ​ 𝐈 ) \bm{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\Delta_{{\bm{h}}}^{2}\mathbf{I}) . Here, Δ 𝒉 \Delta_{\bm{h}} denotes the global sensitivity —the maximum L 2 L_{2} difference between outputs on two neighboring datasets—and σ \sigma controls the noise level as a function of ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) . By adding noise calibrated to sensitivity, the Gaussian mechanism ensures that the presence or absence of any single sample only has a limited influence on the output. This mechanism underlies differentially private training methods such as DP-SGD ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) , and, as we will show, it also directly connects to the diffusion sampling process we analyze in this work. As an interesting fact in differential privacy, it is widely known that subsampling amplifies privacy ( Kasiviswanathan et al., 2011 ) . For example, if we flip a coin to decide whether each entry of the training data is in or out to form a smaller dataset, we would expect the mechanism using the smaller dataset to be twice as private as the original mechanism using the full dataset. With a flipping probability of 50 % 50\% , every individual benefits from perfect privacy if the individual is not included in the smaller dataset. To benefit from the privacy amplification effect, a subsampled Gaussian mechanism (applying the Gaussian mechanism on randomly subsampled data) is also widely used ( Abadi et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 2019 ) . We will also study the effect of subsampling on the privacy loss incurring during the diffusion sampling process.

sections.text: While the Gaussian mechanism provides a natural foundation for analyzing privacy, the classical ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -DP framework yields only loose bounds when these mechanisms are composed, often resulting in substantially looser guarantees than the actual privacy loss. To address this, we adopt the more refined f -DP framework ( Dong et al., 2022 ) , which characterizes privacy through hypothesis testing and provides an exact trade-off curve (function), rather than the looser worst-case bounds of ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -DP. A particularly important special case is Gaussian Differential Privacy (GDP) , which describes the privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism exactly using a single parameter μ \mu . sections.heading: Appendix M Broader Impact Statement
sections.text: This work studies privacy leakage that can arise during diffusion-based sampling and provides tools for quantifying how individual training records may influence generated outputs. Its primary positive impact is to support more privacy-aware deployment of generative models, especially in settings where training data may contain sensitive or proprietary information. By shifting attention from only differentially private training to sampling-time privacy accounting, the proposed framework may help practitioners design generative pipelines that better balance privacy and utility, for example through subsampling, early stopping, or hybrid use of public denoisers. This can make formal privacy analysis more accessible for large-scale diffusion systems where fully private training remains costly or impractical. At the same time, the work has limitations and possible risks. The formal guarantees are derived for an empirical denoiser with tractable sensitivity, while modern deployed systems typically use neural denoisers whose exact data sensitivity remains difficult to characterize. As a result, the analysis should not be interpreted as a complete privacy certificate for arbitrary diffusion models. If misused or overstated, sampling-time privacy estimates could give a false sense of security. Moreover, improving the privacy–utility tradeoff of generative models may also make it easier to deploy high-quality synthetic data systems in sensitive domains, where failures could still expose private information or amplify biases present in the underlying data. We therefore view this work as a step toward, rather than a substitute for, end-to-end privacy evaluation. Responsible use should combine sampling-time accounting with empirical privacy audits, membership-inference evaluation, dataset governance, and clear reporting of assumptions. More broadly, our analysis highlights that privacy in generative modeling is shaped not only by training, but also by how samples are produced, released, and reused.

While differentially private (DP) training provides formal guarantees, it comes at a cost in sample quality. In this work, we study a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred during the sampling process itself? Directly analyzing modern neural denoisers is challenging because their sensitivity to a single training example is generally intractable. To overcome this challenge, we construct and analyze a clipped privacy-accountable empirical denoiser , a training-free estimator of the Bayes-optimal denoiser, whose per-step sensitivity can be computed explicitly, allowing each denoising step to be a Gaussian mechanism. This perspective enables privacy accounting under Gaussian DP when each training example contributes to each denoising step, and under f f -DP trade-off functions when each generated sample uses a single randomly subsampled block of the training data. We report every ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) guarantee as a certified upper bound from a privacy loss distribution accountant, and use a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation as a fast diagnostic, characterizing where it is reliable and where it becomes anti-conservative. We also analyze the privacy loss along the denoising trajectory and show that it grows steeply near the critical window in which semantic content is formed. This observation motivates hybrid samplers that use the private empirical denoiser through the formative steps where it remains a faithful proxy for the neural denoiser, then switch to a public neural denoiser for the remaining refinement. Our results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 show that the privacy of diffusion models depends not only on the training procedure, but also on sampling-time design choices such as subsampling, stopping time, and hybrid denoising. 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) are now central to modern generative systems, but their ability to reproduce training examples raises serious privacy concerns ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Carlini et al., 2023 ; Tang et al., 2024 ; Hu & Pang, 2023 ; Duan et al., 2023 ; Matsumoto et al., 2023 ) . Post-hoc filters and memorization-aware model changes can reduce visible leakage, but they do not give attack-agnostic privacy guarantees. Differentially private (DP) training gives such guarantees, but it answers a different question: it bounds what the weights reveal, while users and regulators see only generated samples. Sampling-time leakage is a separate surface that persists even when the denoiser is trained non-privately, whether or not DP training is practical at scale. This raises a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred by the sampling process itself? Answering this requires treating the sampler, rather than the training algorithm, as the mechanism to be analyzed. The obstacle is that a neural denoiser has intractable data sensitivity, so its denoising steps admit no explicit privacy accounting. To make the problem analyzable, we privatize an empirical denoiser ( Niedoba et al., 2025 ) whose sensitivity can be computed directly. Since each reverse diffusion step already injects Gaussian noise, the empirical denoising update can be interpreted as a Gaussian mechanism, allowing us to track the sampling trajectory with Gaussian Differential Privacy (GDP) ( Dong et al., 2022 ) . However, the GDP composition using the full batch of training data yields a poor privacy level. Denoising with subsampled data at each denoising step can improve the privacy level. However, this hurts the diffusion sampling, as every newly drawn subset of data injects extra stochastic drift into the sampling trajectory, which prevents coherent semantics from forming across the trajectory. To this end, we propose output-wise subsampling , subsample a block from the dataset once and reuse it for the entire denoising trajectory to produce one sample. This stabilizes the denoising direction and achieves a decent privacy level. When converting f f -DP to ( ϵ , δ ) (\epsilon,\delta) -DP, we encounter unreliable conversion, especially at small δ \delta , when using the CLT-type f f -DP accounting that assumes the CDF of the standardized test statistic under the composition is simply Gaussian. We report all guarantees as certified upper bounds from a PLD accountant ( Doroshenko et al., 2022 ) , and study a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation ( Zheng et al., 2020 ) as a fast estimate and measure where it is accurate and where it understates the certified value. DP training of diffusion models builds on DP-SGD ( Abadi et al., 2016 ; Dockhorn et al., 2023 ; Ghalebikesabi et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) and protects the weights at a cost in sample quality. Private sampling has mostly been studied for Bayesian posterior inference, where the samples are model parameters rather than data ( Welling & Teh, 2011 ; Wang et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2019 ; Räisä et al., 2021 ; Zhang & Zhang, 2023 ) . Bertazzi et al. (2025) show that privacy loss in SGLD can concentrate in the final step, but their analysis needs strongly convex, Lipschitz objectives, which our empirical denoiser does not satisfy. Sampling-time privacy for diffusion models. Closest to our setting, Sehwag et al. (2023) also analyze privacy at generation rather than training time, clip denoiser outputs, treat each step as a Gaussian mechanism, and delegate late denoising to a public model. Our analysis differs in three respects. First, their per-step sensitivity C / k C/k arises from a sample-and-aggregate ensemble of k k non-private models trained on disjoint shards, so the sensitivity floor is set by the ensemble size and private training is still required; we obtain sensitivity 2 ​ C / | 𝒟 | 2C/|\mathcal{D}| by clipping individual contributions to a single empirical average, with no training at all. Second, they adopt a per-sample private-prediction threat model and name composition across multiple released samples as open; we give an explicit joint-release guarantee over N out N_{\mathrm{out}} outputs under standard DP, using subsampled f f -DP with block-level amplification. Third, we localize privacy loss to the critical window and place the handoff at the measured crossover rather than at a fixed schedule fraction, validating the choice with a membership-inference proxy. Wei et al. (2023) study inherent privacy properties of discrete denoising diffusion and likewise find that leakage concentrates at particular stages of generation. Their mechanism is the discrete transition kernel, while ours is the continuous Gaussian reverse SDE, where the noise already injected by the sampler serves as the mechanism noise. Our results are therefore a continuous-state counterpart to their staged view, and our claims are scoped accordingly. Empirical denoisers. Niedoba et al.
